Bittern Station has ninety days of air, and the loop that is supposed to be sealed is handing back water it never took in — 2.3 kilograms too many, every day, for eleven days running. Nobody aboard can make water without spending oxygen or hydrogen already spoken for, and forty days before the surplus began, the station's second electrolysis stack died, leaving six people breathing down a reserve that empties on a date Nora Pike can already estimate. She is the only one who can key the distress call that would end the mystery and the mission both, and she will not sign for numbers she has not watched accumulate herself. Around her, a mine engineer who trusts nothing with a screen, a medic who will not report a figure without its error bar, a life-support tech counting reserve oxygen by hand each morning, and a recycler technician guarding a logbook whose founding number turns out to have never been a reading at all — five people working the same shaft from five directions, one pipe at a time, one sample at a time, toward a source that may also be what killed the first stack. A tug is sixty-one days out, already loaded with a replacement part nobody aboard requested. Someone, somewhere, already knows what is wrong. This is a mystery told in gauge readings and logbook entries, where the clue that saves six lives is a number nobody wanted to be right.

For readers of *The Martian*, *2010: Odyssey Two* and *The Expanse*.
# Chapter 1 — The Second Strip

The 0600 handover smelled of carbonate, the way every hour aboard did, sweetish and faintly mineral, worked so far into the collar of Pike's coverall that she only noticed it when Salas came close enough to hand her the strip.

He had signed it. The signature sat in the box at the foot of the printout, and above the signature the numbers ran in two columns, inlet and outlet, hour by hour through the night watch. Salas had not read them. Pike knew this the way she knew the pitch of the number three circulation pump, which had been running a half-tone flat since she came on rotation and would run flat until someone replaced a bearing nobody had: by long exposure, without needing to prove it. He signed what he was handed. That was not a failing in a relief hand. It was the whole job description.

"Quiet," Salas said.

"Quiet's fine."

He went aft to sleep. Pike stood under the sodium strip in the recycler alcove and read the printout properly, which took ninety seconds, and then she folded it in three and put it in her breast pocket with the others.

There were ten in there already. Day −11 through the night before last, the fold lines soft now from being carried, each one annotated in her own hand in the margin where Cold Harbor's schema had no field. The eleventh made eleven. Inlet 61.0 kg through the pass. Outlet 63.3. Difference plus 2.3, and it was 2.3 the way the previous ten had been 2.3 — not 2.28 rounded up, not 2.31 shaded down, but the same figure walking in every morning wearing the same coat.

She did the accumulation in her head because she had done it every morning for six days and the answer arrived before the arithmetic did. Eleven days at 2.3 was 25.3 kg. On 61 kg of throughput, 2.3 was a shade under 3.8 percent. The tolerance on the loop, entered in the standing instruction on the day the station was commissioned and never argued with since, was half a percent over any twenty-four-hour window. She was running seven and a half times tolerance and had been running it for a week and a half, and the totalizers themselves counted to two hundredths of a kilogram per pass, which meant the instrument had no room to be lying at that magnitude. A totalizer could drift. It could not invent 2.3 kg eleven mornings running and hit the same figure each time.

Nothing was being created. That was the part she kept coming back to. In a loop sealed downstream of the slurry isolation valve, with one metered way in, more out than in was not luck. It was a door somebody had not drawn on the plan.

At 0640 she went forward to the command module and took the binder off its clip.

The logged strips lived in order, tabbed, the paper stiffer than hers because it had never been in anyone's pocket. She pulled Day −11 and worked forward. Marchetti's hand was small and level and he wrote the same way every day, which was the quality Cold Harbor had trained into him and the quality they had picked him for.

Day −11: *loop inventory 612 kg. Δ within tolerance.* Signed, G. Marchetti.

Day −10: *loop inventory 612 kg. Δ within tolerance.*

She went through all eleven. Every one read 612. Every one read inside tolerance. Six hundred and twelve kilograms was the number the previous watch had entered, and the watch before that, and it had never in the station's life been an instrument reading; it was a figure that lived in the schema and got carried forward because the field required something. And for the last six days — since her own strip and the logged strip had quietly stopped agreeing — nobody had said a word about it, including her.

That was the piece she had to hold. She had not raised it either. She had carried the paper in her pocket for six days waiting for the accumulation to become loggable under station rule, five days minimum before a totalizer difference could be entered as a finding, and the rule had been satisfied on Day −6 and she had gone on carrying it for five more. There was a version of this where she had been careful. There was another version, and she was not yet certain which one she was in.

At 0900 the watch took the wardroom for the morning brief. Pike laid the eleven logged strips in a row down the table, and beneath them, aligned by date, her own eleven. She sat down and did not speak.

Vance got it in four seconds. She counted them, because she wanted the number.

"Yours say plus two-three," he said. "His say six-twelve and fine."

"They do."

"Every day?"

"Eleven days. Twenty-five point three kilos we did not put in."

Vance did not go for the summary screen on the bulkhead. He turned his hand over and read off the back of it, where he had pencilled the morning count of the reserve dewars, the way he did at 0500 before anyone else was up and had done every morning since Stack B went into its bag.

"One hundred eighty point zero," he said. "Six of us at zero-eight-five is five point one a day. Stack A at sixty percent derate gives me three point one. That's a two-kilo shortfall a day, every day, and at two kilos a day one-eighty is ninety days. Ninety. And that's if nothing else breaks." He tapped the pencil marks. "Every hour Stack A is off the line costs me point one three of a kilo off that. Not off the day. Off the ninety."

"I know."

"Then declare. Seal the modules, put us in suits, sit the rotation out on the bottles and let somebody come and get us. Nora, we don't know what's crossing into that loop. Stack B's membranes fouled, they didn't age. Stack A is downstream of the same water."

"If I key it, it's transmitted," Pike said. "Not discussed. Thirty-one minutes to Cold Harbor and then it's irrevocable, and the claim opens to the first hull that reaches us. That's not a safety action. That's a property transaction I can't take back."

"And ninety days is ninety days."

"Ninety days is ninety days of time to spend," she said. "I'm spending five of it."

She opened the log and wrote the finding, because eleven days of accumulated totalizer difference was loggable and a tank level was not, and she had never in two rotations signed a level.

Okoye to the slurry line: valve position, physically felt, and the line temperature the full three hundred metres. Brede to the spectrometer: D/H on loop water, on seam ice, on bottled feedstock, error bars attached. Marchetti to produce every schema entry since Day −11, unrounded, with the source of the 612.

She signed it. Five days.

Then she stood, and left her own strip lying on the table where she had put it, instead of folding it back into her pocket.
# Chapter 2 — Inside Tolerance

The printer in the command module was older than anyone aboard and it printed the way it always had, four lines a second, so that eleven days of Cold Harbor schema came off the roller slowly enough for Marchetti to read them as they arrived. He did not want to read them as they arrived. He stood with his hands flat on the bench and let the paper feed over the edge and into the catch tray, and the sweetish carbonate smell came off the warm rollers with the paper, the way it came off everything.

Eleven entries. Day −11 through Day −1, and then the two Pike had opened the finding across, which made thirteen sheets in the tray and eleven of them his.

He lifted them out and squared the edges against the bench and went down the right-hand margin with a finger, because the signature block on the Cold Harbor schema sits low and right, under the environmental fields, where a man does not look at it unless he is looking for it.

G. MARCHETTI, RECYCLER TECH. Eleven times. Under each one, in field 14, LOOP INVENTORY (KG): 612.

He had known that. He had known it the way you know the pitch of a pump — as a condition of the room and not a fact about it. Seeing it stacked was different. Field 14 was mandatory. He had built a career of small exactitudes on the understanding that mandatory meant the form required a number, and that supplying a required number was not the same act as asserting one. He put his thumb on the field and tried, on the screen, to leave it blank. The schema returned the entry with the field boxed in red and the word REQUIRED. He tried the flag character the Consortium used for provisional values, the caret, and the schema stripped it and returned 612 and would not accept the entry until he acknowledged that it had. There was no comment field attached to field 14. There was a comment field attached to field 22, water quality, and one attached to field 31, consumables, and the schema did not let a comment cross a field boundary.

So the form permitted exactly one statement about the loop inventory, and it was 612, and it was mandatory, and he had made it eleven times over his own name.

He went back for the origin of it, because that was the disciplined thing and because he wanted very much for it to have an origin.

The handover entry, Day −300. Pike's signature as officer of the watch, his own as incoming custodian. Field 14: 612, and beside it in the provenance column the notation CF — carried forward. He opened the prior watch's final entry. Field 14: 612, CF. The watch before that, 612, CF. He went back through fourteen months, and then another fourteen, and then he stopped opening entries one at a time and queried the field across the whole station record, and the schema gave him a column of 612 that scrolled for a long time without changing a digit, all the way down to commissioning, where field 14 read 612 and the provenance column read DESIGN.

Not measured. Designed. The wet volume of the loop as drawn, before anyone filled it.

He searched the maintenance record for an ultrasonic reading of the potable loop and found none. There was no station history of anyone putting a transducer on it. There was no fitting to put one on. Level was read on the tanks at ±1.5%, which on a 600 kg tank was ±9 kg and useless for this, and the loop itself was a sealed circuit of pipe and membrane stack and surge bottle that nothing aboard had ever looked into. The number the whole watch had reasoned from — the number Pike had subtracted 25.3 from in her head at the brief, the number he had defended — had never been produced by an instrument. It was a drawing. It was sixty years of men copying a drawing and signing it.

He sat down with that for a while. The pumps went on doing what they did.

Then he did the other thing, the one he had been putting off, which was to reconstruct his own rounding.

He laid the totalizer strips beside the schema entries and worked them day by day. Day −11: inlet 61.0, outlet 63.3, difference +2.3 on 61 kg throughput, which was +3.8% against a ±0.5% daily tolerance. He had entered the day inside tolerance. His reasoning was written in his own margin annotation in his own hand: *TOT ±0.02/pass, mult. passes, within instr.* The instruments counted to ±0.02 kg per pass and the loop made many passes a day, and he had argued to himself, defensibly, that a stack of small uncertainties could grow to cover 2.3 kg, and that a discrepancy inside instrument tolerance was not yet a fact, and that a man does not put not-yet-facts into a Consortium record.

Day −10, +2.3. Day −9, +2.3. He wrote them down the margin of a blank strip in a column because he wanted to see it the way Pike had made him see it, as a column and not as a series of days each of which had been reasonable.

Eleven days. 2.3, eleven times, was 25.3 kg.

And in field 14, eleven times, he had entered the change as nothing at all. Not wrongly. That was the part he kept returning to and could not get past: every single entry was defensible on its own, and the form had no way to hold the sum, and so the sum had gone into the only place available to it, which was nowhere.

He was still sitting there when he opened the transmission log, out of the same mechanical thoroughness, to see what the Consortium had been sent while all this was not being recorded.

The log was mostly nothing. Scheduled schema pulls, one a week, a few hundred kilobytes each, no human hand on them. He scrolled back past Day −11, past Day −29 —

And stopped.

0412, Day −29. AUTO SCHEMA PULL — CH. Not a scheduled one. An unscheduled pull, triggered on content, and the content line listed the fields it had taken, and among them was field 09, EQUIPMENT FAULT, carrying the stack-fault flag. Marchetti knew that flag intimately. He had set it himself on Day −40, in this chair, the evening Vance bagged Stack B, because the schema required a fault flag on a failed unit and he was loyal to the form.

Sent by no one. Acknowledged by Cold Harbor thirty-one minutes later, which was simply how far away they were. And within the day, on a manifest he had no business having seen and had seen anyway, on the Kestrel loading list: one electrolysis stack, membrane type, Bittern spec.

Eighteen days before the loop began coming back rich, a machine at Bittern had told a machine at Cold Harbor something no one aboard had decided to say. Twenty-nine days before Pike put her strip on the table.

He looked at it for a long time. Then he closed the transmission log without printing it.

He took the 612 to Pike in the galley and put the commissioning entry in front of her with the provenance column showing, and said that the number was a drawing and had never been measured and that he had signed it eleven times. She read it twice and said, "All right. That's a finding." She did not ask what else he had opened. He did not offer it.

Vance came through with the morning count on a card in his fist, 176.0 kg, and said it to the room the way he said it every morning: four kilos off the one-eighty in two days at two a day, eighty-eight days at the same draw, and the draw had not changed.

Marchetti went back to the command module and opened the Day +2 entry to sign it.

Field 14 was already filled in. 612. Provenance: CF.
# Chapter 3 — A Valve You Can Feel

Salas tended the lock, because tending the lock was what Salas did when he was not on the 0200 watch, and because Okoye did not want Vance doing it. Vance would have stood at the panel with the consumable board up and read the cost of the trip out loud twice, once before and once after, and Okoye had already done that arithmetic on paper at 0530 and did not need it recited.

One eighty had been the number on Day 0. Six days at two a day was twelve, which put the dewars at 168.0 kg before he so much as touched the inner hatch. Two cycles to get out and back, 0.9 kg of atmosphere apiece, 1.8 kg total, of which 0.4 kg was oxygen. That left 167.6. Before the trip, 168.0 at the unchanged 2.0 kg/day draw had been 84.0 days still to run, and six days spent plus eighty-four to come was ninety on the nose — the number the strip had carried since Day 0. The station's rule gave that ninety twelve cycles of slack, 2.4 kg of oxygen, before it had to become eighty-nine, and two cycles, 0.4 kg, did not touch it. But that rule was cut for a gauge — ±1.5 percent of 180 kg, the better part of three kilograms either way, noise a hand ledger does not carry. He had not read a gauge. He had counted kilograms one cycle at a time since Day 0, and by that count the remainder was 167.6 exactly, 83.8 days, and six plus 83.8 was 89.8. A gauge could have called that ninety and stayed inside its own error. A pencil could not. The strip on the command module bulkhead was wrong from the moment he cracked the seal and would have to be re-cut.

He wrote 167.6 on the back of his glove checklist in pencil so he would not have to take anyone's word for it later.

Salas ran the fit check. Okoye did the last of it himself anyway — wrists, neck ring, the left knee seal that had been weeping argon-dry talc for a month — because a fit check you watch on a display is a report and a fit check you do with your thumbs is a fit check. The pumps changed pitch as the lock drew down, that long descending complaint, and then there was no pitch at all, only the suit, and 0.028 g, and the dark.

Ceres does not make a landscape out of its dark. It makes a floor. He went up the cut at a walking pace that would have been a fall anywhere else, the regolith taking his boot and giving it back with nothing like conviction, and the slurry line ran beside him the whole way, jacketed, lagged, strapped at two-metre intervals to a rail he had bolted himself in his first month.

Three hundred metres. He put a glove on every jacket section.

That was the point of coming. The line had forty-one heater zones and every one of them reported a temperature to a screen inboard, and Okoye had never once signed a heater figure off that screen, because a thermocouple tells you what the thermocouple is doing and a glove tells you what the line is doing. He worked up the run section by section, palm flat, counting three seconds, feeling the warmth come through the layup as a slow pressure rather than a heat. Section eleven. Section twelve. The jacket at zone nineteen was hotter than its neighbours and he stopped there and knew exactly why before he checked the local dial: Day −14, a slug in the line, and he had raised the zone setpoint fourteen degrees to drive it through and clear the head.

The dial said fourteen degrees high. He had left it there. Twenty days.

He had logged it as a slug. That was all he had logged — *slug cleared, zone 19, line normal* — because at the time there had been nothing else true to write. A setpoint is not a finding. A setpoint is a thing you do to a line to make it behave, and he had done it, and then a stack had failed forty-six days back and a loop had started coming back rich seventeen days back and nobody had asked him what temperature the line was running at, because nobody had thought the line was in the question.

He stood with his glove on zone nineteen for longer than three seconds.

Then he went on to the isolation valve, because that was the other thing he had come for and the only thing he would sign today.

The log said full open. The log had said full open for three hundred days. Okoye got both gloves on the stem and felt the collar, and the stem was out — out to the shoulder, out to the stop, the threads bare and cold and gritty with fines the way an open stem is. He worked the handwheel a quarter turn shut and a quarter turn back and felt the packing drag and then release. Full open. Confirmed the only way it can be confirmed, which is with a hand on it. He would sign that.

It was turning away from the valve body that he found the other thing.

Downstream of the inlet totalizer — downstream, on the loop side, past the point where anything entering the potable system is supposed to have been counted — there was a tie-in. Fifteen millimetres, maybe. A short jacketed stub off the crown of the line, running up and aft in a lazy arc and then in through the gland plate toward the recycler house, toward the vapour-compression stage. It was strapped, it was lagged, it was neat. Somebody had built it on purpose and built it well.

It was not on any drawing aboard Bittern. He had all of them memorised, the as-builts and the commissioning set and the two revision sheets, and there was no line on any of them off the crown of the slurry line between the totalizer and the gland plate. There had never been.

He put his glove on it.

Warm. Not line-warm, not zone-warm — a thinner heat, the heat of something moving fast through a small bore, and the stub carried a faint high tremble into his palm that pipe does not do when it is carrying liquid. Liquid shoves. Liquid thumps and surges. This whispered. He held it for ten seconds by the suit clock, then moved his hand forty centimetres along and held it again to be sure it was not sun and not a heater strap, and there was no sun here and no strap there, and it was still warm.

He did not say anything on the loop. Salas was on the loop.

He took his samples last, because samples are the part you do when your hands are already tired and you want them done right. Two chips. One off the fresh face, from the lens he had advanced the head into on Day −96, prying with the flat of the chisel until a palm-sized wafer came away in that slow falling way that nothing on Ceres ever finishes. One off the worked-face product where it sat on the billet rail, hard and clean and old.

He bagged them, sealed them, and wrote on the labels with the grease pencil: FACE, LENS, D−96 ADVANCE, DAY +6. And: BILLET RAIL, WORKED FACE PRODUCT, DAY +6.

Location and date. Nothing else. He thought he knew what the first one was and he was not going to write his thinking on a label that was going to end up in Brede's hand, because Brede would read it, and Brede would then be measuring a sample that had already been told what it was. Let the vials say it or let them not.

Two cycles spent. Ten left in the budget.

He came inboard damp, still in the undersuit, hair flat, the carbonate sweetness on him worse than usual, and he went to the watch desk with the two bags in one hand and the pencilled checklist in the other before he had even racked the hard shell.

"Full open," he said. "Stem out. I felt it. You can log that."

Pike waited.

"There's a tie-in," Okoye said, "off the crown of the line, downstream of the inlet totalizer. Fifteen mil. Goes into the vapour-compression stage. It is not on any drawing on this station and it is warm and it is not carrying liquid — you can feel that it isn't."

"Meaning."

"Meaning the inlet totalizer counts litres." He set the bags on the desk, squarely, side by side. "It's a liquid flow meter. It counts liquid going past it at plus or minus two hundredths of a kilo a pass, and it does that honestly, and it has been doing it honestly for three hundred days. That stub is carrying steam." He wiped his face with the back of his wrist. "Nothing aboard Bittern has ever counted steam as anything at all."

Somewhere aft a pump changed pitch, and four people heard it, and nobody looked up.

"And 167.6," he said. "Re-cut the strip. Eighty-nine, by count, not by gauge."
# Chapter 4 — Without a Baseline

The medical bay ran four degrees colder than the rest of Bittern because the spectrometer wanted it that way, and Hannah Brede had long ago stopped bringing a jacket. Cold hands were steadier. She had the two chips Okoye had brought her laid out on the anodized tray, each in its own foil sleeve, each labelled in his blunt hand with a location and a date and nothing else. No guess. No note saying *I think this is the one*. She had asked him for that on Day +6 and he had looked at her as though she had asked him not to breathe, and then he had done it.

She burned the worked face first.

Five millilitres, degassed, reduced over hot chromium, into the source. The instrument took eleven minutes to settle and she used them to write the run number, the date, the sleeve label and the cell temperature into the bound logbook, because the spectrometer's own memory held ninety runs and then began to eat the oldest, and she did not intend to lose a number to a ring buffer.

Worked face: 171 ppm D/H, ±10.

She wrote it with the error bar attached, because a number without one was a rumour.

The second chip was from the new lens — the carbonate Okoye had cut into ninety-six days ago and logged as a face change. Bound water, driven out of the mineral itself under the torch. It took longer to prepare and she was careful with it, because there had been twenty-two vials in the drawer when all this began and she had just spent two.

820 ppm, ±10.

She sat back on the stool and looked at the two numbers for a while with the fans going and the condensate crawling down the cold face of the bulkhead behind her.

Six hundred and forty-nine ppm apart.

That was luck, and she knew exactly how much of it she had been handed. Two reservoirs in the same crater, cut from the same seam by the same head, and they were separated by a factor of nearly five. If the lens had come in at 200 ppm she would have had nothing — no instrument aboard could have told the two apart, and the whole question of where the water came from would have stayed a story people told each other in the wardroom. Instead the seam had handed her a tracer. She did not believe in providence. She wrote *649 ppm separation — tracer viable* in the margin and moved on.

Then she ran the potable loop.

213 ppm, ±10.

She looked at that one for a long time too, and then she capped the vial, logged the run, and did not tell anybody.

Vance found her before the 1800 handover, which she had expected, because Vance counted his LOX by hand every morning and a man who did that could not help wanting numbers from other people.

"You ran the loop."

"I ran a sample of the loop."

"And?"

"And I'm not reporting it."

He waited. He was good at that, which was rarer aboard than he knew.

"Two hundred and thirteen parts per million," she said, "plus or minus ten. And that figure means nothing, Theo, and I want you to understand *why* it means nothing before you carry it out of this compartment, because you will carry it out of this compartment."

"It's six hundred short of the lens."

"It's forty-two above the worked face. Against what?" She turned the logbook so he could see the empty column. "There is no archived loop sample aboard this station from before Day minus eleven. I've been through the medical stores, the assay locker and Marchetti's sample racks. Nothing. Not one 5 ml vial of loop water from a day when the loop behaved. So I have a number, and I do not have the thing that makes a number a measurement. I don't know what this loop read on Day minus twenty. It could have sat at 213 since commissioning. It could have sat at 160. An offset without a baseline is not a measurement. It's a number with a story attached, and the story is the part you'd be carrying."

Vance took that. He did not like it. The two were separate operations with him.

"Then get a baseline."

"There isn't one to get. It's gone. It went out the outlet totalizer three hundred days ago." She put the pen down. "So I stop measuring the offset and I measure the slope instead."

That was the part she had worked out at 0300 with the pumps changing pitch through the deck.

A rate of change needed no baseline. If the seam was pushing 2.3 kg/day of 820 ppm water into a 612 kg loop sitting near 171, the loop had to *climb* — 2.3 times the difference, over the inventory, a shade under two and a half ppm every day. Call it 2.44. Thirteen days of that was thirty-two ppm, and thirty-two ppm was three times her error bar and visible from the far end of the compartment. One sample against nothing was invisible. Thirteen paired samples regressed against day number was an experiment her instrument could actually win, and it was the only one.

She needed the feed side clean first. Carryover from the outlet header would blur the paired samples and there was no point in starting a thirteen-day series with a dirty swab.

Vance broke Stack A for six hours so she could do it.

He wrote the cost on the strip before he opened the breaker, not after — 3.1 kg/day, six hours, a quarter of a day, 0.78 kg — in his own hand, with the time and his initials, while the stack was still running. Then he pulled it. Brede watched him do it and understood that this was the thing Vance had instead of an error bar.

At the wardroom she gave them the accounting the way it stood. One hundred and eighty at Day 0, less two a day for eleven days was 158.0. Less the 0.4 kg of oxygen Okoye had vented on his two cycles: 157.6. Less 0.78 for the outage: 156.8 kg. At 2.0 kg/day that was 78.4 days. Day +11 plus 78.4 landed on Day +89.

Then she told them what she would not give them.

"Paired samples, loop and outlet, every day for thirteen days. I will have nothing before then. Not a trend, not a sense of it, not a feeling. I am asking the watch not to request a preliminary opinion in the interval, because if you ask me on day six I will either refuse you or I will guess, and the second one is worse."

Pike said, "Noted," and wrote it down, which was Pike's entire vocabulary for agreement.

Brede started the series that night with six vials.

Vance did the subtraction out loud, the way he did everything.

"Twenty-two. Two on Sam's chips. One on the loop. Six now." He looked up. "Thirteen left."
# Chapter 5 — Cell Voltage, Morning

At 0527 Vance was already in the LOX bay with the ullage sheet on the clipboard and a pen he had carried since before the rotation, because the pens aboard leaked in the cold and this one did not. He did not turn on the summary screen. That was the whole of his method and he had never once explained it to anyone, because explaining it would have made it sound like superstition instead of what it was, which was the refusal to let a number tell him what to see before he had seen it.

Dewar one. He put his hand flat on the outer jacket first, the way he had since Day −40, feeling for the frost band and finding it where it had been yesterday and a finger's width lower. Ullage pressure, 118 kPa. Level by the ultrasonic, and he wrote the raw figure and then the ±1.5 % beside it in the margin because the number without its error was a rumour. Dewar two, warmer side, frost band lower again. Pressure 117. He wrote both.

Then the arithmetic, in pen, on paper, the same seventeen lines he had written seventeen mornings running.

One hundred eighty point zero at Day 0. Two point zero a day, because six people breathe 5.1 and Stack A at sixty per cent derate makes 3.1 and the difference comes out of these two bottles and nowhere else. Seventeen days is thirty-four. That is 146.0. Less the two airlock cycles Okoye spent walking the line on Day +6, which vented 0.9 kg of atmosphere each and 0.2 kg of that oxygen, so 0.4. That is 145.6. Less the 0.78 Stack A did not make in the six hours Vance had broken it so Brede could swab the feed side, which he had signed for and would sign for again.

144.8.

He looked at it a moment. Then he woke the screen, and the screen said 144.8, and he felt the small clean satisfaction of a man whose paper had been right and who would have believed the paper anyway.

Seventy-two point four days at the present draw. Day +17 and seventy-two point four is Day +89. He wrote *89* and circled it, which he had done every morning for seventeen mornings, and the circle had moved by exactly nothing, which was the only good news the station had.

It was 0554. The 0600 watch would not want the bay. Vance sat down on the toolbox with the clipboard on his knee and, for no reason he could name afterwards except that the number 89 had been obedient and he had a spare six minutes, pulled Stack A's cell-voltage history.

He had not looked at it since Day −40. That was the point of a derate: you set it, the stack runs inside it, and you stop looking, because looking at a thing that is behaving is how you talk yourself into running it harder. He pulled forty days because forty was the habit-number, and then extended it because the file went back further, and then he stopped moving.

1.82 volts on Day −40. 1.824. 1.828. 1.832.

He counted along it with the pen tip and did not write anything for a while. Four millivolts a day. Not a scatter, not a step, not the ragged thing a fouled cell does when it is dying in patches. A line. Fifty-seven points with a rule laid along them.

Cell voltage climbs when the membrane resists. The stack is drawing the same current and paying more for it, and a derate does not do that; a derate is a ceiling, and this was a floor rising to meet one. He wrote: *1.82 + 57 × 0.004*. He did the multiplication longhand because it was 0559 and he wanted to be wrong. 0.228. 2.048.

He went to the panel and read live cell voltage off the instrument itself, hand on the housing, the way he read everything.

2.05.

Vance sat back down. Stack B's record was in the same archive, forty days stale and never touched since he had bagged the brick and written the label. He would not open the bag. He had told Pike that on Day 0 and he meant it this morning more than he had then. But the file was not the bag. He scrolled Stack B to its last hour and read the number it had been holding when it quit taking current.

2.10 volts.

From 1.82 at four millivolts a day, 2.10 is seventy days. Day −40 plus seventy.

Day +30.

He wrote it and then wrote the rest of it, because the rest of it was only subtraction and he had never in his life stopped a subtraction halfway. Thirteen more days from this morning at 2.0 a day is 26.0 off 144.8. One hundred eighteen point eight kilograms standing on Day +30. And on Day +30 Stack A makes nothing at all, so the draw is not 2.0, it is the whole 5.1, six people at 0.85 each with nothing coming in.

118.8 over 5.1. He did it twice. Twenty-three point three days.

Day +30 plus twenty-three is Day +53.

Kestrel arrives Day +61.

He sat with the clipboard and the two circles on it, the 89 he had drawn at 0554 and the 53 he had drawn at 0603, and understood that the 89 had never been a number about oxygen. It had been a number about Stack A holding, and Stack A had been telling him for fifty-seven mornings, in four-millivolt increments, exactly when it would stop.

Eight days. On the wrong side.

Kestrel called at 1140, nineteen minutes of light-lag each way now, which made it less a conversation than a pair of letters read aloud. The voice was unhurried and pleasant and used the watch by name: hoped Pike was getting sleep, asked whether Brede had vials enough, said the replacement stack was in the hold, bagged, seals intact, and that they had checked it that morning against the manifest. Then, at the end, in the same register as the rest: *And we can burn early the instant Bittern declares. Say the word and we shave days off. No pressure from us either way.*

Vance logged the traffic. He did not answer it; Pike answered traffic.

He did not go to her that night.

He thought about it through the 1800 and most of the 2200, and what stopped him was not fear and not doubt about the arithmetic. It was that he had been the one shouting on Day 0 to declare, and he had been overruled by a woman who would not sign a tank level, and she had been right not to sign it. A slope through fifty-seven points was not five days of accumulation. It was a projection. If he carried it to Pike at 2300 with his voice still up from Kestrel's call, it would arrive as the same argument he had already lost, wearing better clothes.

So at 2340 he tapped it through the bulkhead instead, in the old knock-code the two of them had fallen into weeks ago because Marchetti's pump ran loud and neither of them slept. Numbers went slowly. *2.05. 2.10. Day 30.*

A long pause. Then, from the other side, one word tapped out patiently, letter by letter: *tolerance*.

Vance put his knuckle against the cold plate and tapped back: *slope*.

Nothing after that. They lay in adjacent compartments with forty-one metres of regolith overhead, listening to each other's pumps hold their pitch, until Salas came through at 0200 for the relief and the sound of the hatch made them both, separately, pretend to be asleep.
# Chapter 6 — The Bag

The last pair went into the inlet at 0540, and Brede logged the time before she logged the number, because the time was the only thing she was certain of yet.

Thirteen days. Day +11 through Day +24, one loop sample every morning at the same point in the same watch, paired with an outlet sample on the days she could afford one. She had not been able to afford all of them. Nineteen vials on Day +11 — twenty-two at the start of all this, less two spent on Okoye's chips from the worked face, less one on the first loop run that told her nothing she could sign — and the series had eaten fifteen. Four left in the rack, standing in their foam like teeth in a jaw. On five of the thirteen days she had skipped the outlet sample and written *outlet omitted, vial ration* in the margin of the run sheet in her own hand, because the alternative was a series that looked complete and was not, and she would rather hand Pike a gapped series than a tidy lie.

She ran the regression on paper first. She always did. The screen would give her the same answer in a quarter second and she would not believe it until she had seen the residuals herself, spread across thirteen rows, none of them large, none of them leaning.

Slope: 2.38 ppm per day. Standard error on the slope: 0.30.

She sat with that for a moment in the warm noise of the med bay, the condensate running its slow bead down the cold face of the bulkhead behind the spectrometer, and did the division. Two point three eight over point three zero. Seven point nine.

"Seven point nine," she said aloud, to the empty room, and then, because it would be read by people who needed a word and not a decimal, "eight. Call it eight."

She wrote the sentence out once, crossed it out for a hedge she did not like, and wrote it again.

*Loop D/H is increasing at 2.38 ± 0.30 ppm per day over thirteen days, non-zero at approximately eight standard errors. This is a slope. It is not, by itself, a cause.*

She signed it. The word *cause* was absent on purpose and she wanted anyone reading to feel its absence like a missing tooth. A slope was a correlation with a direction. What made it a mechanism was somebody else's evidence, and she did not have it yet.

Then she turned the arithmetic inside out, which was the part she had been waiting thirteen days to do.

Pike came at 0700 and stood where she always stood, one hand on the frame, not touching the bench.

"Say it small," Pike said.

"Small first, then the useful one." Brede turned the sheet round. "If 2.3 kilograms a day of water at 820 ppm is entering a loop holding L kilograms at 171, the loop's ratio climbs by 2.3 times 649, divided by L, every day. That's forced. The only unknown on the right is L."

"And you've got the left."

"I've measured the left. 2.38." She wrote it. "So L equals 2.3 times 649 over 2.38. Fourteen ninety-two point seven over two point three eight. Six hundred and twenty-seven kilograms."

Pike did not move. "Error bar."

"Twelve point six percent on the slope carries straight through. Twelve point six percent of 627 is seventy-nine. Six hundred and twenty-seven, plus or minus eighty."

"Six-twelve," Pike said.

"Six-twelve is inside it. So is six-twelve plus the twenty-five point three Marchetti rounded away — that's six three seven point three, and it sits closer to my centre than the design figure does." Brede put the pencil down. "Nora. Six-twelve has never been measured. Not at commissioning, not since, not by anything. There's no fitting to measure it with. This is the first instrument estimate of the loop inventory anyone aboard Bittern has ever made, and it is an estimate, and it has an eighty-kilogram bar on it. But the water Gil has been rounding out of the log is in the loop. It's been in the loop the whole time. What went missing was the record."

Pike looked at the sheet for longer than she needed to. "That's a slope," she said. "Not a cause."

"That's what I signed."

Vance brought the cause at 0930, and he brought it in a bag.

He carried it through from the workshop held out from his body the way you carry something that might still be alive, and set it on the med bay bench: Stack B, sealed and labelled in his own block capitals on Day −40, forty days of not opening it, and now twenty-four more. The seal came apart with a crack that Brede felt in her teeth.

"I expected grey," he said.

They were not grey. Membranes that had died of age came out grey and thinned and soft at the folds, and these came out white — crusted, matte, a bloom across the active face like frost that had been dried onto it and then dried again.

Brede swabbed two square centimetres and ran it.

"Sodium carbonate," she said. "Not wear. Scale."

Vance sat down. It was the only time she had seen him do that.

He took Stack A off the line at 1100 for its own feed-side swab, and before he pulled the breaker he wrote the cost on the strip, the way he always did, the figures small and upright: *full day, 3.1 kg. 180.0 less 24 days at 2.0 = 132.0, less 0.4 less 0.78 less 3.1 = 127.7. At 2.0/day, 63.8 days. Day +87.* He drew a line through *eighty-nine* on the board and wrote *eighty-seven* above it, and he wrote it before he opened the breaker and not after.

Stack A's membranes came out white too. Thinner scale, a lighter bloom, the same crystal under the loupe — forty days behind and going the same way at the same rate.

Pike came back at 1600 and asked for the one-line version.

Brede gave it with the bars in it, because there was no version of it that was true without them.

"The fresh lens has been handing us two things down the same tie-in. Scale since Okoye cut the new face on Day −96, and water since he raised zone nineteen fourteen degrees on Day −14. The scale is on Stack B and it is starting on Stack A. The water is 2.3 kilograms a day into a loop I now measure at 627 ± 80. Same pipe. Same vapour. One source." She waited. "Close the isolation valve and the scale stops. Close the isolation valve and the water stops. It is one motion. There is no valve position that gives us one and not the other."

Pike said, "And the water is what we've been drinking."

"The water is what we've been living on," Brede said. "Since Day −11. Sixty-one kilos a day through the loop and two point three of it free, and the free two point three is the thing that is killing the stacks."

The pumps went on making the noise they had made all day. Nobody had put that water there. That was the whole finding, and the price of it was the water.
# Chapter 7 — Thirty-Three

The sheet was the back of a totalizer strip, cut square and turned over. Pike ruled it down the middle with the edge of the pencil and wrote **KEY** on the left and **HOLD** on the right, and then sat for a while with the pumps going and did not write anything else, because the two columns were not the hard part. The hard part was that they were both arithmetic and only one of them could be undone, and it was not the one she wanted.

Left column first.

*Key at 2300. CH has it 2331. Early burn authorised or not authorised inside twenty-four hours — assume authorised, Kestrel wants it. Arrival Day +47.* Under that: *claim open at 2331. First hull alongside. Kestrel is the only hull.*

Right column: *Do not key. Kestrel Day +61 on present trajectory. No burn available after today — the window closes with the phasing.*

Then across the bottom, under both, the line that made the sheet worth ruling at all. She wrote it out longhand because she wanted to see the words rather than the digits.

*Vance: Stack A cell voltage 1.82 V Day −40, +4 mV/day, straight. Stack B quit at 2.10 V. Stack A reaches 2.10 on Day +30.* Day +30 was three days ago. *After that Stack A makes nothing and the draw goes 2.0 to 5.1.*

And the standing number, which she did in the margin in her own hand the way she had done every morning since Day 0, not because she doubted Vance's column but because a number you have not subtracted yourself is a number you are quoting.

180.0 start. Thirty-three days at 2.0 the day, the standing shortfall, the term that ate everything: 66.0. That left 114.0, and 114.0 was where the arithmetic stopped being a subtraction and started being a history.

Less 0.4, Okoye's two cycles on Day +6, the walk that found the tie-in.
Less 0.78, Brede's six hours with Stack A down on Day +11.
Less 3.1, the full day down on Day +24, the day they opened the bag.
Less 0.4, the two cycles Okoye was going to spend this morning, which she had authorised at 0615 and which she entered now rather than later because she did not keep two sets of figures.

109.3 kg.

At 2.0 kg/day: 54.6 days. Day +33 plus 54.6 was Day +87, and she wrote *+87* and boxed it, and looked at the box, and saw what she had been seeing for a week. The four subtractions below the line came to 4.68 kg between them. The standing draw came to 66.0. Every argument aboard this station had been about the 4.68.

Day +87 was only true while the draw stayed 2.0.

Marchetti knocked on the frame at 0910 and did not come in, which was how he knocked.

He had one sheet too. He put it on the table face down, turned it over, and stepped back before she could read it, and that was the first thing that told her what it was.

The transmission log. An unscheduled automatic pull, Cold Harbor origin, 0412 on Day −29, and in the payload the stack-fault flag with the schema field beside it filled in and initialled *G.M.*

"No human sent that," he said. "The pull is automatic. But the field is mine. I filled it Day −40 because the schema requires it filled inside seventy-two hours of a plant fault, and the pull took it out at 0412 on the twenty-ninth, and Kestrel loaded a stack inside the day. I have had this since Day +2. I gave you the six-twelve and I kept this." He put his hands behind him. "I'd like to stand down from the log. Salas can keep the schema. I'll show her the entry rules this afternoon."

"No," Pike said.

He waited.

"You filled a field you were required to fill. If you'd left it blank the schema would have flagged you on Day −37 and someone else would have filled it on Day −36." She turned her own sheet over so he could see the box and the figure in it. "And the same schema is why six-twelve stood for ten years without an instrument on it. It carried the number forward because carrying forward is what the form does, and it carried the fault out because carrying out is what the form does. It did both. Your name is at the bottom of both." She set the pencil down. "You don't get to stand down from one of them. You'd be standing down from the wrong one."

"I rounded eleven entries."

"You did. That cost us five days and it is in the log in your hand and mine, and you will keep making the entries, because the next person to make them will make them worse and I will not be able to tell." She looked up. "Stand down when it stops mattering who fills the field. It hasn't stopped."

Okoye went out at 1055 and was at the valve at 1140. He called it through on the suit loop, flat, the way he called everything: isolation valve, hand wheel, thirty-one turns, hard stop, confirmed by feel through the glove. Then the plate — fifteen millimetre, jacketed, cut that morning on the bench, blanked at the flange downstream of the inlet totalizer. Four bolts. He read the torque out twice.

It stopped the vapour into the loop. It also stopped the slurry, and therefore the boiler, and therefore the billets, and therefore the contract tonnage, and therefore the +2.3 kg/day that was the only generous number on the station. One hand wheel and four bolts had closed all of it in the same motion, and Pike wrote *1140 isol. valve closed, tie-in blanked, S. Okoye* and beneath it *0.4 kg, two cycles. Eight remaining.*

Cold Harbor answered the previous day's query at 1622, sixty-two minutes late against the thirty-one each way. *Continue working the face at present rate. Book surplus as yield. No fault condition indicated.*

She logged it verbatim, every word, including *no fault condition indicated.* Then she logged beneath it that the officer of the watch had disregarded the instruction, that the face had been isolated at 1140, that the surplus was bound water from an uncounted carbonate lens crossing a liquid-only totalizer, and that the same vapour had scaled Stack B's membranes to failure and was forty days into Stack A's. She signed the instruction. Then she signed the disregard, separately, with the time on each.

At 2300 the command module was hers. The key was live. The declaration sat composed on the pad, eleven words, and thirty-one minutes on the far side of them.

She read her sheet again. Day +47 was inside the line. Day +61 was eight days outside it. Day +87 was only true while the draw stayed 2.0, and the draw stayed 2.0 only while Stack A held, and Stack A had passed 2.10 volts three days ago and had not quit — which meant either Vance's line was straight and Stack A was living on borrowed slope, or the line had bent when the vapour stopped.

Three days would tell her which. Three days cost 6.0 kg and the early burn.

She did not key it. She wrote instead: *Watch held to a Stack A cell voltage re-read, 0600 Day +36, T. Vance and N. Pike present. Distress not keyed this date. Early-burn window forgone knowingly.* She signed it.

Then she took the eleven strips out of her pocket, the ones that had never matched the logged ones, flattened them on the console, and entered all eleven into the permanent record — Day −11 through Day 0, each with its date, each marked BACKDATED, each initialled *N.P.* It took forty minutes. It was the same offence she had been holding against Marchetti since Day 0, and she entered it in her own hand, and signed that too.
# Chapter 8 — What Goes in the Entry

The 0600 handover pad came up from Salas with four lines on it and nothing else, which was correct. Marchetti set it beside the four voltage strips he had printed the night before and laid them out on the mess table in order, left to right, the way he laid out everything: Day +36, Day +44, Day +52, Day +60.

2.01 V. 1.94. 1.85. 1.79.

He read the gaps rather than the numbers. Eight days from the first to the second was seven hundredths; eight days to the third was nine; eight days to the last was six. A rise that had run four millivolts a day for seventy-six days had stopped rising somewhere in the eleven days after Okoye's plate went on, turned over, and come down harder than it had ever gone up. This morning's read was 1.79 V. On Day −40, with Stack B still a working machine in the next frame, Stack A had stood at 1.82.

Below where it started. That was the thing he kept coming back to, pen uncapped over the margin, not writing yet. Vance had measured 2.05 on Day +17 and drawn the line forward to 2.10 on Day +30 and told them all that Stack A was going to quit on a Tuesday. Stack B had quit at 2.10. Stack A had gone to about 2.02 and turned around, because the scale had stopped arriving and the membrane had begun, slowly, in the way of membranes, to clear.

He wrote in the margin of the Day +60 strip: *climb flattened ~D+44, reversed. 1.79 V vs 1.82 V at D−40. Below commissioning-era working point.* Then he capped the pen, because the next number was not his to produce.

Vance brought it at 0620, in his own handwriting on a torn sheet, as he had brought it every morning for sixty days: the reserve dewars counted down by hand, valve by valve, gauge by gauge, no display trusted.

67.3 kg.

Marchetti did the subtraction on the pad where anyone could follow it, because the two terms were the entire chapter of the last four weeks.

109.3 standing at 1140 on Day +33, when the valve went shut. Three days after that at the old shortfall, 2.0 kg/day, because nobody had re-read the stack yet and the log does not get to assume: 6.0 kg. Then twenty-four days from the Day +36 re-read to this morning at 1.5 kg/day, because from the re-read forward the recovery was a measurement and not a hope: 36.0 kg.

109.3 − 6.0 − 36.0 = 67.3.

It closed to the tenth against a hand count made with a torch and a wrench in a cold compartment. That almost never happened.

"It agrees," Marchetti said.

"I know it agrees." Vance had not sat down. "It agrees because the stack is making three point six."

"Five point one demand. One point five short. Yes. Three point six."

"The log carries three point one."

"Since Day minus forty."

"Then the log is wrong and I'm not signing it." Vance's hands were at his sides and open, which with him meant he had already thought it through. "Gil. Put three point six in that field and Cold Harbor reads it as headroom. They read it as the stack being fine, and the next thing in the manifest is a tonnage figure that assumes it. I have spent this whole finding refusing to sign anything that says Stack A can be run harder. I'm not going to sign it on the day it finally looks good."

"You counted the dewar."

"I counted the dewar. I'll sign the dewar. Sixty-seven point three, my hand, my name." He put the torn sheet down on the table and squared it, once, with two fingers. "I won't sign the rate that produced it."

So Marchetti had, laid out in front of him, a measured number and a signed number half a kilogram a day apart, and one field in the schema to put one of them in.

He worked it both ways in the margin, because that was the only honest thing to do with it. 67.3 divided by the signed 2.0 was 33.6 — thirty-three days, rounding the way the schema rounded, down. 67.3 divided by the measured 1.5 was 44.9 — forty-four days. Eleven days between a number that was true and a number that was signed. On Day −11 he had rounded 2.3 kg/day to nothing eleven times and it had cost five days. He wrote both figures. He left both on the pad.

Brede came through at 0740 with the rack under her arm and set it down so he could see into it. One vial. She had gone in with four.

"Three on the post-closure loop," she said. "Day plus thirty-four, plus forty-seven, plus fifty-nine. Regressed against the thirteen-day series."

"And?"

"Zero point one, plus or minus zero point three, parts per million per day." She said it the way she said everything, the error bar welded to the number, refusing to be quoted without it. "Which is flat. It is not zero. It is indistinguishable from zero at the precision of this instrument, and I will sign it as flat within error and nothing stronger."

Before Day +33 the loop had been enriching at 2.38 ± 0.30 ppm/day for thirteen consecutive days. After the plate went on the fifteen-millimetre tie-in, it was doing nothing at all.

"It stopped on the day," Marchetti said.

"It stopped on the day and, as far as three vials can tell, within the hour." She picked the rack back up. "That's the confirmation. It's also the cheapest number anybody has produced on this station."

Kestrel called at 0210, four minutes of lag now, close enough that the pauses felt like manners rather than distance. Salas took it on the 0200 and wrote it out on the pad in block capitals, the way Salas wrote everything, and signed underneath:

KESTREL ALONGSIDE D+61 APPROX 1500. ASKS AGAIN IF BITTERN WISHES TO DECLARE PRIOR TO ARRIVAL. SAYS NO PRESSURE. SAYS STACK IS IN THE HOLD EITHER WAY.

Salas had no opinion about it, and had written none, and had gone off watch.

Pike gave him the entry at 0900 and left the compartment, which was its own instruction.

The schema opened with the field pre-populated: LOOP INVENTORY 612 KG, provenance DESIGN, carried forward three hundred days and every day before that back to commissioning. Marchetti selected it and typed over it.

**627 ± 80 kg — measured.** Provenance: INSTRUMENT, D/H regression, thirteen-day series, Brede.

Then, because the schema would not ask and a custodian was supposed to: NOT A TOTALIZER ACCUMULATION. DOES NOT MEET THE FIVE-DAY DIFFERENCE BAR FOR A LOGGED FINDING. NO INSTRUMENT ABOARD CAN WEIGH THIS LOOP AND NONE EVER HAS BEEN FITTED. ENTERED AS THE ONLY MEASUREMENT OF THIS QUANTITY EVER MADE ON BITTERN, AT ITS STATED ERROR, IN PREFERENCE TO A DESIGN FIGURE AT NO STATED ERROR AT ALL.

Under DISPOSITION he filed 25.3 kg of seam-origin water as product recovered — not yield, not surplus, product — flagged against an assay that could no longer stand, and entered the requirement: VINALIA SEAM FOUR ASSAY TO BE RERUN, BOUND WATER IN CARBONATE FRACTION NOT PREVIOUSLY COUNTED.

Then he opened Day −96 and amended Okoye's entry from a face change to an assay change, and let the schema do what it did with an amendment that old, which was to raise a flag on every entry between.

In the production field he put 3.6 kg/day, provenance INSTRUMENT, and beneath it Vance's 2.0, provenance SIGNED, and the two air figures, forty-four and thirty-three, side by side with the divisors shown.

He signed it. His name went at the bottom of that one too.
